title: André Bessette (early January)
hookLine: a sickly doorkeeper in Montreal who welcomed thousands and built a shrine to Joseph

lines: A KNOCK AT THE DOOR IN MONTREAL.
A THIN MAN TAKES YOUR COAT.
THEY SHOWED HIM THE DOOR. HE STAYED.
cards: A knock at a school's front door in Montreal. A small, thin man in a religious habit opens it. He takes your coat, asks who you've come to see, and lets you wait by the stove.
He does this all day. He sweeps the floor, runs errands, cuts the students' hair. He can barely read.
His health was so poor that his religious order nearly sent him away. He later joked that his superiors showed him the door, and he stayed there.

teach.b: André Bessette was a brother of the Congregation of Holy Cross in Quebec; people called him Brother André. He was weak from childhood, had little schooling, and worked odd jobs before he entered religious life.
His community hesitated to keep him, but they did, and made him porter, the doorkeeper of their college in Montreal. A doorkeeper sees everyone: students, parents, the sick, the poor, the curious.

teach.h: HE PRAYED WITH THE SICK TO JOSEPH.
teach.b: André had a deep love for Saint Joseph, the quiet carpenter, and he began to pray with people who came to the door with troubles, especially the sick.
He would encourage them to pray to Joseph, and sometimes rubbed them with oil from a lamp burning before Joseph's statue. People said they were healed.
Crowds started coming to the door, then to a small wooden chapel he wanted built on the slope of Mount Royal.

teach.h: A SMALL CHAPEL GREW INTO AN ORATORY.
teach.b: That chapel grew, over his lifetime and after it, into Saint Joseph's Oratory, a great basilica above the city. André never took the credit.
He insisted it was Joseph, and God, who healed; he was only the one who opened the door.

teach.h: I HAVE CHOSEN TO BE AN ABJECT IN THE HOUSE OF MY GOD.
teach.b: There's a psalm line he could have hung over his post, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have chosen to be an abject in the house of my God, rather than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners."
An abject is the lowliest person there; in some translations, a doorkeeper. Pope Benedict declared him a saint. The man they nearly sent away is buried in the shrine he started.

how: Catholics honor Saint André Bessette in early January; pilgrims visit Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, where he is buried, and some pray there with oil blessed in Saint Joseph's name.

games.q: you're Brother André. crowds now come to your door saying you healed them. what do you say?
o: accept the thanks; you prayed hard.
send them away so you can work.
it was Saint Joseph, and God, not me.
games.why: he kept pointing past himself, to Joseph and to God. the crowds kept coming anyway, and the chapel grew into an oratory.

practice: Think of the doors in your day, your front door, an office door, the message you open, the call you pick up, and picture one person who will come through one of them. See their face before they arrive.
If you pray, ask Saint Joseph, or Brother André, to pray for them; if not, simply decide now to greet them well.
